source_refs.note: Practice MCQs written from Chapter 21 (PDF 75-87, printed 72-84); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Chapter 21 (Halogenoalkanes), arranged by the chapter's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation; numerical questions show the working.

blocks.prompt: 1 In the past, chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) were mainly used as:
blocks.explanation: CFCs were used as refrigerants and aerosol propellants; they are now being replaced (introduction).

book_ref.quote: chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) were used as refrigerants and aerosol propellants

blocks.prompt: 2 CFCs are being replaced by eco-friendly alternatives such as:
blocks.explanation: The book says CFCs are being replaced by eco-friendly alternatives such as Freons (introduction).

book_ref.quote: though these are being replaced by eco-friendly alternatives such as Freons

blocks.prompt: 3 Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) contain the elements:
blocks.explanation: As the name says: chloro (chlorine), fluoro (fluorine) and carbon (introduction).

book_ref.quote: chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) were used as refrigerants and aerosol propellants

blocks.prompt: 4 The halogen-containing polymer used for non-stick cookware is:
blocks.explanation: Halogenoalkanes are intermediates for polymers such as PVC for piping and PTFE (Teflon) for non-stick cookware (introduction).

book_ref.quote: PTFE (Teflon) for non-stick cookware

blocks.prompt: 5 PVC (polyvinyl chloride), made from halogenated intermediates, is used mainly for:
blocks.explanation: PVC is used for piping and PTFE for non-stick cookware (introduction).

book_ref.quote: PVC (polyvinyl chloride) for piping

blocks.prompt: 6 Halothane is widely used as:
blocks.explanation: Halothane is a powerful inhalation anesthetic that induces a reversible loss of consciousness during surgeries (introduction).

book_ref.quote: Halothane is a halogenated hydrocarbon widely used

blocks.prompt: 7 The halogen atoms present in a halothane molecule (CF₃–CHClBr) are:
blocks.explanation: The structure of halothane has a carbon with three F atoms bonded to a carbon carrying Cl, H and Br (introduction).

book_ref.quote: It induces a reversible loss of consciousness during surgeries

blocks.prompt: 8 Chloroform and other chlorinated anesthetics are now banned because of:

options.text: their inability to cause loss of consciousness

blocks.explanation: Chloroform and other chlorinated anesthetics are banned now due to their toxicity and safety concerns (introduction).

book_ref.quote: which are banned now due to their toxicity and safety concerns

blocks.prompt: 9 A halogenoalkane is formed when, in an alkane:

options.text: one or more carbon atoms are replaced by halogen atoms
a halogen molecule adds across a double bond only
an –OH group replaces a hydrogen atom
one or more hydrogen atoms are replaced by halogen atoms

blocks.explanation: A halogenoalkane is formed when one or more H atoms of an alkane are replaced by halogen atoms (introduction).

book_ref.quote: is formed when one or more hydrogen atoms of an alkane are replaced by halogen atoms

blocks.prompt: 10 Dichloromethane, CH₂Cl₂, is classified as a:
blocks.explanation: Halogenoalkanes are mono, di, tri or poly depending upon the number of halogen atoms; CH₂Cl₂ has two (introduction).

book_ref.quote: depending upon the number of halogen atoms

blocks.prompt: 11 Monohalogenoalkanes are also called:
blocks.explanation: Monohalogenoalkanes are also called alkyl halides, general formula R – X (introduction).

book_ref.quote: monohalogenoalkanes are also called alkyl halides

blocks.prompt: 12 In the general formula R – X of alkyl halides, X stands for:

options.text: a halogen atom (F, Cl, Br, I)

blocks.explanation: R may be methyl, ethyl, propyl etc. and X represents halogen atoms F, Cl, Br, I (introduction).

book_ref.quote: where R may be methyl, ethyl, propyl, etc., and X represents halogen atoms

blocks.prompt: 13 Monohalogenoalkanes are classified as primary, secondary and tertiary on the basis of:

options.text: the type of carbon atom bearing the halogen atom
the total number of carbon atoms

blocks.explanation: They are classified depending upon the type of carbon atom bearing the halogen atom (introduction).

book_ref.quote: depending upon the type of carbon atom bearing the halogen atom

blocks.prompt: 14 Chloromethane, CH₃Cl, is a primary halogenoalkane because its halogen-bearing carbon is attached to:

options.text: one halogen and two carbon atoms

blocks.explanation: In a primary halogenoalkane the C–X carbon is attached to one or no carbon atom; in CH₃Cl it is attached to none (introduction).

book_ref.quote: the halogen atom is attached with a carbon which is further attached to one or no carbon atom

blocks.prompt: 15 Which of these is a primary halogenoalkane?
blocks.explanation: In 1-chloropropane the C–Cl carbon is attached to only one carbon, so it is primary; the book's examples are chloromethane, chloroethane and 1-chloropropane (introduction).

book_ref.quote: Examples of primary halogenoalkanes

blocks.prompt: 16 2-Chlorobutane, CH₃–CHCl–CH₂–CH₃, is a:
blocks.explanation: Its C–Cl carbon is attached directly to two other carbon atoms, so it is secondary (introduction).

book_ref.quote: Examples of secondary halogenoalkanes

blocks.prompt: 17 2-Chloro-2-methylpropane, (CH₃)₃C–Cl, is tertiary because the carbon bearing Cl is attached directly to:
blocks.explanation: In a tertiary halogenoalkane the halogen-bearing carbon is attached to three carbon atoms directly (introduction).

book_ref.quote: the halogen atom is attached to a carbon atom which is further attached to three carbon atoms directly

blocks.prompt: 18 Ethane reacts with chlorine in the presence of light to give:
blocks.explanation: Halogenation of alkanes in light: CH₃–CH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃–CH₂–Cl + HCl (21.1).

book_ref.quote: Halogenoalkanes can be prepared by the halogenation of alkanes in the presence of light

blocks.prompt: 19 The reaction H₂C=CH₂ + HBr → CH₃–CH₂–Br is an example of:
blocks.explanation: Halogenoalkanes can be prepared by electrophilic addition of hydrogen halides to alkenes; ethene gives bromoethane (21.1).

book_ref.quote: electrophilic addition of hydrogen halides to alkenes

blocks.prompt: 20 In the conversion CH₃–CH₂–OH + HCl → CH₃–CH₂–Cl + H₂O, ZnCl₂ acts as:
blocks.explanation: Alcohols are converted to alkyl halides by halogen acid in the presence of ZnCl₂, which acts as a catalyst (21.1).

book_ref.quote: in the presence of ZnCl₂ which acts as a catalyst

blocks.prompt: 21 When ethanol reacts with thionyl chloride, the catalyst used is:
blocks.explanation: Alcohols react with thionyl chloride in pyridine as a catalyst to give alkyl chlorides (21.1).

book_ref.quote: react with thionyl chloride in pyridine as a catalyst to give alkyl chlorides

blocks.prompt: 22 The thionyl chloride method of making chloroalkanes is especially useful because:

options.text: it gives an alkene as a by-product
its by-products, HCl and SO₂, are gases that escape, leaving the pure product

blocks.explanation: CH₃CH₂OH + SOCl₂ → CH₃CH₂Cl + SO₂ + HCl; the gaseous by-products go off leaving the pure product (21.1).

book_ref.quote: the by-products (HCl and SO₂) are gases which go off leaving behind the pure product

blocks.prompt: 23 Ethanol reacts with PBr₃ to give bromoethane and:
blocks.explanation: 3CH₃CH₂OH + PBr₃ → 3CH₃CH₂Br + H₃PO₃ (21.1).

book_ref.quote: Phosphorus trihalides or phosphorus pentahalides react with alcohols

blocks.prompt: 24 How many moles of ethanol react with one mole of PBr₃?
blocks.explanation: 3CH₃CH₂OH + PBr₃ → 3CH₃CH₂Br + H₃PO₃: three –OH groups are replaced by the three Br of one PBr₃ (21.1).

book_ref.quote: react with alcohols to replace – OH group by a halo group

blocks.prompt: 25 The products of the reaction of ethanol with PCl₅ are:
blocks.explanation: CH₃CH₂OH + PCl₅ → CH₃CH₂Cl + POCl₃ + HCl (21.1).

book_ref.quote: Phosphorus trihalides or phosphorus pentahalides react with alcohols

blocks.prompt: 26 When an alcohol is heated with KBr and H₂SO₄, the species that actually converts the alcohol into a bromoalkane is:

options.text: HBr formed from KBr and the acid

blocks.explanation: The acid first reacts with KBr to give hydrogen bromide, which then reacts with the alcohol to give the bromoalkane (21.1).

book_ref.quote: The acid first reacts with potassium bromide to give hydrogen bromide

blocks.prompt: 27 Besides bromoethane, the products of CH₃CH₂OH + KBr + H₂SO₄ are:
blocks.explanation: CH₃CH₂OH + KBr + H₂SO₄ → CH₃CH₂Br + H₂O + KHSO₄ (21.1).

book_ref.quote: This method is commonly used to prepare bromoalkanes and iodoalkanes

blocks.prompt: 28 Phosphoric acid rather than sulphuric acid is preferred for preparing iodoalkanes because phosphoric acid:

options.text: is a gas at room temperature
reacts with alcohols to give alkenes only
is a weak oxidizing agent, less likely to oxidize I⁻ to I₂

blocks.explanation: Phosphoric acid is preferred for iodoalkanes because it is a weak oxidizing agent and less likely to oxidize iodide ions to iodine (21.1).

book_ref.quote: less likely to oxidize iodide ions to iodine

blocks.prompt: 29 Marine algae and phytoplankton such as Trichodesmium convert seawater bromide into:
blocks.explanation: These organisms convert seawater bromide into volatile organobromides, which take part in the global bromine cycle (21.1, Interesting Information).

book_ref.quote: These organisms convert seawater bromide into volatile organobromides.

blocks.prompt: 30 Experiments show that the main factor deciding the reactivity of halogenoalkanes is:

options.text: the strength of the carbon–halogen bond
the size of the alkyl group only
the boiling point of the compound

blocks.explanation: The strength of the C–X bond is the main factor; the weaker bond breaks more easily and makes the molecule more reactive (21.2).

book_ref.quote: the strength of carbon halogen bond is the main factor which decides the reactivity of haloalkanes

blocks.prompt: 31 In a halogenoalkane molecule R – X, the partial charges are:

options.text: δ– on the carbon, δ+ on X
δ+ on X and on the carbon
δ+ on the carbon attached to X, δ– on X

blocks.explanation: R – X has an alkyl group with a partial positive charge on the carbon attached to the halogen and a partial negative charge on the halogen (21.2).

book_ref.quote: an alkyl group with a partial positive charge on the carbon atom attached to halogen atom

blocks.prompt: 32 According to Table 21.1, the strongest carbon–halogen bond is:
blocks.explanation: Bond energies: C–F 467, C–Cl 346, C–Br 290, C–I 228 kJ/mol; C–F is the strongest (21.2).

book_ref.quote: Table 21.1 Bond energies of different C-X bonds

blocks.prompt: 33 Using Table 21.1, by how much is the C – Cl bond energy greater than the C – Br bond energy?

book_ref.quote: Table 21.1 Bond energies of different C-X bonds

blocks.prompt: 34 From Table 21.1, the difference between the strongest and the weakest C – X bond energies is:
blocks.explanation: Strongest C–F 467, weakest C–I 228: 467 – 228 = 239 kJ/mol (21.2).

book_ref.quote: Table 21.1 Bond energies of different C-X bonds

blocks.prompt: 35 For the same alkyl group, the correct order of reactivity of halogenoalkanes based on C – X bond strength is:
blocks.explanation: Iodo compounds have the weakest bonds and are most reactive; fluoro compounds least: R–I > R–Br > R–Cl > R–F (21.2).

book_ref.quote: iodo compounds (with the weakest bonds) would be the most reactive halogenoalkanes

blocks.prompt: 36 Under ordinary conditions, fluoroalkanes:

options.text: do not react, because the C – F bond is very strong
react only by the SN1 mechanism

blocks.explanation: The C – F bond (467 kJ/mol) is so strong that fluoroalkanes do not react under ordinary conditions (21.2).

book_ref.quote: the C – F bond is so strong that fluoroalkanes do not react under ordinary conditions

blocks.prompt: 37 Besides bond strength, which of the following is NOT listed in the chapter as a factor affecting the reactivity of halogenoalkanes?
blocks.explanation: Other factors are bond polarity, steric hindrance and inductive effect (21.2).

book_ref.quote: Some other factors which may affect the reactivity of halogenoalkanes are, bond polarity, steric hindrance, inductive effect

blocks.prompt: 38 The C – X bond in halogenoalkanes is polar because:

options.text: both atoms have the same electronegativity
carbon and the halogen differ in electronegativity
the halogen has no lone pairs

blocks.explanation: The C-X bond is polar due to the difference of electronegativity between C and the halogen atom (21.3).

book_ref.quote: is polar due to the difference of electronegativity between C and the halogen atom

blocks.prompt: 39 In a halogenoalkane, the carbon of the C – X bond behaves as:

options.text: a nucleophilic centre attacked by electrophiles
an electrophilic centre attacked by nucleophiles

blocks.explanation: The carbon of C-X acts as an electrophilic centre which can be attacked by a nucleophile (21.3).

book_ref.quote: acts as an electrophilic centre, which can be attacked by a nucleophile

blocks.prompt: 40 Elimination (E) reactions of halogenoalkanes involve:

options.text: removal of HX to form alkenes
replacement of X by a nucleophile
addition of HX to form alkanes

blocks.explanation: Elimination reactions involve the removal of HX from halogenoalkanes and result in the formation of alkenes (21.3).

book_ref.quote: involve the removal of HX from halogenoalkanes

blocks.prompt: 41 In a nucleophilic substitution (SN) reaction of a halogenoalkane:

options.text: HX is removed and an alkene forms
a hydrogen atom is replaced by the halogen
the halogen is replaced by another atom or group
two molecules of the halide join

blocks.explanation: SN reactions are those in which the halogen is replaced by some other atom or group; the halogen leaves as X⁻ (21.3).

book_ref.quote: Those reactions in which the halogen is replaced by some other atom or a group

blocks.prompt: 42 In the general SN reaction Nu⁻ + R–X → R–Nu + X⁻, the species X⁻ is called the:
blocks.explanation: The drawing labels Nu⁻ as the attacking nucleophile, R–X as the substrate, R–Nu as the substituted product and X⁻ as the leaving group (21.3).

book_ref.quote: Nucleophilic substitution reaction (original drawing

blocks.prompt: 43 The two main processes in nucleophilic substitution on alkyl halides are:

options.text: breaking of the C – X bond and formation of the C – Nu bond
formation of a C=C bond and loss of HX
breaking of a C – H bond and formation of a C – X bond
addition of X₂ and loss of H₂

blocks.explanation: The processes are departure of the leaving group (C – X bond breaking) and attack of the nucleophile (C – Nu bond formation) (21.3.1).

book_ref.quote: the departure of leaving group (breaking of C – X bond) and the attack of nucleophile

blocks.prompt: 44 If the breaking of the C – X bond and the formation of the C – Nu bond occur simultaneously in a single step, the mechanism is:
blocks.explanation: Simultaneous bond breaking and bond formation in a single step is the SN2 mechanism; in two steps it is SN1 (21.3.1).

book_ref.quote: If the two processes occur simultaneously in single step the mechanism is called SN2

blocks.prompt: 45 In the SN2 mechanism, the extent of bond formation is:

options.text: equal to the extent of bond breaking
greater than the extent of bond breaking

blocks.explanation: As soon as the nucleophile starts attacking, the C – X bond starts breaking; the extent of bond formation equals that of bond breaking (21.3.1).

book_ref.quote: the extent of bond formation is equal to the extent of bond breaking

blocks.prompt: 46 In the SN2 mechanism, the nucleophile attacks the electrophilic carbon:

options.text: from the same side as the leaving group
only after the leaving group has gone
from the side opposite to the leaving group

blocks.explanation: The nucleophile attacks from the side opposite to the leaving group (backside attack) (21.3.1).

book_ref.quote: It attacks from the side which is opposite to the leaving group

blocks.prompt: 47 SN2 is called bimolecular because:

options.text: two molecules take part in its single, rate-determining step

blocks.explanation: The reaction takes place in one step, which is the rate-determining step, and two molecules participate in it (21.3.1).

book_ref.quote: two molecules are participating in this step, it is a bimolecular reaction

blocks.prompt: 48 The rate equation of an SN2 reaction is:
blocks.explanation: Kinetic studies show that SN2 rates depend on both [alkyl halide] and [nucleophile]: Rate = k[RX]¹[Nu]¹ (21.3.1).

book_ref.quote: depend upon both the concentrations of alkyl halide and the attacking nucleophile

blocks.prompt: 49 The overall order of a typical SN2 reaction is:
blocks.explanation: Order = 1 + 1 = 2; a typical SN2 reaction is a second order reaction (21.3.1).

book_ref.quote: A typical SN2 reaction is a second order reaction

blocks.prompt: 50 For an SN2 reaction, the concentration of the alkyl halide is doubled and that of the nucleophile is tripled. The rate becomes:
blocks.explanation: Rate = k[RX][Nu], so the new rate = 2 × 3 = 6 times the old rate (21.3.1).

book_ref.quote: depend upon both the concentrations of alkyl halide and the attacking nucleophile

blocks.prompt: 51 For an SN2 reaction with k = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹, [alkyl halide] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³ and [nucleophile] = 0.20 mol dm⁻³, the rate is:

book_ref.quote: Mathematically, the rate can be expressed as:

blocks.prompt: 52 Which halogenoalkane always follows the SN2 mechanism when attacked by a nucleophile?
blocks.explanation: Primary monohalogenoalkanes always follow SN2 for steric reasons; bromoethane is primary (21.3.1).

book_ref.quote: primary monohalogenoalkanes always follow SN2 mechanism whenever they are attacked by nucleophiles

blocks.prompt: 53 In a primary halogenoalkane the nucleophile can attack the electrophilic carbon easily because that carbon carries:

options.text: only hydrogen atoms or one carbon atom

blocks.explanation: In primary monohalogenoalkanes the substrate carbon is attached to hydrogen atoms or only one carbon atom, so steric hindrance is small (21.3.1).

book_ref.quote: the nucleophile can approach and attack the electrophilic carbon easily

blocks.prompt: 54 In the SN2 reaction of bromomethane with hydroxide ion, the products are:
blocks.explanation: OH⁻ attacks the carbon of CH₃–Br from the back through a transition state HO---C---Br, giving CH₃OH + Br⁻ (21.3.1).

book_ref.quote: SN2 mechanism: bromomethane and hydroxide ion

blocks.prompt: 55 The first step of the SN1 mechanism is:

options.text: attack of the nucleophile on the carbon
reversible ionization of the alkyl halide to a carbocation
removal of a β-hydrogen by a base
formation of a five-groups transition state

blocks.explanation: The first step is the reversible ionization of the alkyl halide, which provides a carbocation as an intermediate (21.3.1).

book_ref.quote: The first step is the reversible ionization of the alkyl halide

blocks.prompt: 56 The ionization step of the SN1 mechanism takes place in the presence of:

options.text: aqueous acetone or aqueous ethyl alcohol

blocks.explanation: The first step is the reversible ionization of the alkyl halide in aqueous acetone or aqueous ethyl alcohol (21.3.1).

book_ref.quote: in the presence of aqueous acetone or aqueous ethyl alcohol

blocks.prompt: 57 The intermediate formed in the SN1 mechanism is a:
blocks.explanation: The ionization step provides a carbocation as an intermediate, which is then attacked by the nucleophile (21.3.1).

book_ref.quote: This step provides a carbocation as an intermediate

blocks.prompt: 58 In the SN1 mechanism, the first step is the slow (rate-determining) step because:

options.text: it involves the combination of ions
two molecules must collide in it
it involves the breaking of a covalent bond

blocks.explanation: The first step breaks a covalent bond, so it is slow compared with the second step, the energetically favourable combination of ions (21.3.1).

book_ref.quote: so it is a slow step as compared to the second step

blocks.prompt: 59 SN1 is called unimolecular because:

options.text: only one molecule takes part in the rate-determining step
the nucleophile takes part in the slow step

blocks.explanation: Only one molecule (the alkyl halide) takes part in the rate-determining step (21.3.1).

book_ref.quote: The mechanism is called unimolecular because only one molecule takes part in the rate-determining step

blocks.prompt: 60 For an SN1 reaction, the concentration of the nucleophile is doubled while that of the alkyl halide is kept the same. The rate:
blocks.explanation: SN1 shows first order kinetics, Rate = k[alkyl halide]; the nucleophile does not appear in the rate equation (21.3.1).

book_ref.quote: the rates of such reactions depend only upon the concentration of the alkyl halide

blocks.prompt: 61 In an SN1 reaction, [alkyl halide] is tripled and [nucleophile] is halved. The new rate is:
blocks.explanation: Rate = k[alkyl halide] only, so the rate becomes 3 times; the change in [nucleophile] has no effect (21.3.1).

book_ref.quote: Reactions involving SN1 mechanism show first order kinetics

blocks.prompt: 62 Tertiary monohalogenoalkanes always follow the SN1 mechanism mainly because:

options.text: their C – X bond is the strongest
they form a stable tertiary carbocation
the nucleophile attacks them easily from the back

blocks.explanation: The major reason is the formation of the stable tertiary carbocation; also three bulky groups block backside attack (21.3.1).

book_ref.quote: the major reason is the formation of the stable tertiary carbocation

blocks.prompt: 63 In a tertiary halogenoalkane, the three bulky groups on the electrophilic carbon:

options.text: make the C – X bond stronger
prevent the nucleophile from attacking from the backside of the leaving group
help the nucleophile attack from the back
turn it into a primary halide

blocks.explanation: Three bulky groups prevent backside attack, so the substrate prefers SN1 (21.3.1).

book_ref.quote: three bulky groups attached with the electrophilic carbon prevent the attacking nucleophile

blocks.prompt: 64 The correct order of stability of carbocations is:
blocks.explanation: Tertiary carbocations are more stable than secondary, which are more stable than primary; the methyl carbocation is least stable (21.3.1).

book_ref.quote: Tertiary carbocations are more stable than secondary carbocations

blocks.prompt: 65 The decreasing stability of carbocations from tertiary to methyl is due to a decrease in:

options.text: the positive inductive effect (+I) of alkyl groups

blocks.explanation: Alkyl (CH₃) groups push electrons towards the positive carbon (+I effect); fewer groups, less stability (21.3.1).

book_ref.quote: Decreasing stability order of carbocations due to decrease in positive inductive effect (+I)

blocks.prompt: 66 Since a carbocation is formed in the rate-determining step of SN1:

options.text: the more stable the carbocation, the more easily it is formed
the less stable the carbocation, the faster the reaction
carbocation stability has no effect on SN1
primary halides react fastest by SN1

blocks.explanation: A carbocation is formed in the rate-determining step, so the more stable the carbocation, the more easily it is formed (21.3.1).

book_ref.quote: the more stable the carbocation, the more easily it is formed

blocks.prompt: 67 Whether a secondary halogenoalkane reacts by SN2 or SN1 depends upon:

options.text: the number of hydrogen atoms on the halogen

blocks.explanation: A secondary halogenoalkane can undergo both SN2 and SN1 depending upon the nature of solvent (21.3.1).

book_ref.quote: A secondary halogenoalkane can undergo both SN2 and SN1 reaction mechanism

blocks.prompt: 68 In the SN1 reaction of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, (CH₃)₃C–Br, with OH⁻, the product formed in the fast second step is:
blocks.explanation: In the second step the carbocation (CH₃)₃C⁺ is attacked by OH⁻ to give the product (CH₃)₃C–OH (21.3.1).

book_ref.quote: In the second step, this carbocation is attacked by the nucleophile to give the product

blocks.prompt: 69 In a β-elimination reaction, the atoms removed from the halogenoalkane are:

options.text: two halogen atoms from the same carbon
a hydrogen on the β-carbon and the halogen on the adjacent carbon
a hydrogen and the halogen from the same carbon
two hydrogen atoms from the β-carbon

blocks.explanation: β-elimination removes a hydrogen attached to the β-carbon and the halogen on the adjacent carbon (21.3.2).

book_ref.quote: a hydrogen atom attached to the β-carbon of the alkyl halide and the halogen atom on the adjacent carbon atom are removed

blocks.prompt: 70 The organic product of a β-elimination reaction of a halogenoalkane is:
blocks.explanation: In β-elimination an alkene molecule is obtained instead of a substitution product (21.3.2).

book_ref.quote: Thus, an alkene molecule is obtained instead of a substitution product

blocks.prompt: 71 Elimination reactions of halogenoalkanes:

options.text: never occur when a nucleophile is present
take place along with substitution reactions and often compete with them

blocks.explanation: Elimination reactions take place simultaneously with substitution reactions and often compete with them (21.3.2).

book_ref.quote: These reactions take place simultaneously with substitution reactions and often compete with them

blocks.prompt: 72 In the E2 mechanism:

options.text: a carbocation forms first, then the base acts
the nucleophile attacks the α-carbon from the back
the halogen leaves in a separate slow step
the base removes the β-hydrogen and the leaving group leaves at the same time

blocks.explanation: In E2 the base attacks the β-hydrogen and the leaving group leaves at the same time, forming a C=C bond in a single step (21.3.2).

book_ref.quote: the base attacks the β hydrogen atom and the leaving group leaves at the same time

blocks.prompt: 73 The E2 elimination of bromoethane by a base gives:
blocks.explanation: Base⁻ takes a β-H of bromoethane while Br leaves, giving ethene + H–Base + Br⁻ (21.3.2).

book_ref.quote: E2 mechanism: bromoethane (original drawing

blocks.prompt: 74 The molecularity and the kinetic order of E2 reactions are:
blocks.explanation: Like SN2, the molecularity of E2 is two and it shows second order kinetics: Rate = k[RX]¹[Base]¹ (21.3.2).

book_ref.quote: the molecularity of E2 reactions is also two

blocks.prompt: 75 For an E2 reaction, [alkyl halide] is halved and [base] is doubled. The rate:
blocks.explanation: Rate = k[RX][Base]; new rate = ½ × 2 = 1 times the old rate (21.3.2).

book_ref.quote: these reactions show second order kinetics

blocks.prompt: 76 The first step of the E1 mechanism is:

options.text: fast attack of the base on the β-hydrogen
slow ionization of the substrate to give a carbocation
simultaneous loss of H and X
attack of a nucleophile from the back

blocks.explanation: In E1, like SN1, the first step is the slow ionization of the substrate to give a carbocation (21.3.2).

book_ref.quote: the first step is the slow ionization of the substrate to give a carbocation

blocks.prompt: 77 In the second step of the E1 mechanism:

options.text: the nucleophile bonds to the positive carbon to give an alcohol
the base removes a β-hydrogen from the carbocation to give an alkene

blocks.explanation: In the second step the base attacks the β-hydrogen atom to give an alkene (21.3.2).

book_ref.quote: In the second step, the base attacks the β-hydrogen atom to give an alkene as a product

blocks.prompt: 78 The alkene formed by E1 elimination of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane is:
blocks.explanation: 2-Bromo-2-methylpropane ionizes to the 3° carbocation; the base removes a β-H to give 2-methylpropene (21.3.2).

book_ref.quote: E1 mechanism: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane

blocks.prompt: 79 Primary halogenoalkanes generally undergo elimination by:
blocks.explanation: Primary halogenoalkanes generally follow E2 whereas tertiary halogenoalkanes follow E1 (21.3.2).

book_ref.quote: Primary halogenoalkanes generally follow E2 mechanism whereas tertiary halogenoalkanes follow E1 mechanism

blocks.prompt: 80 Secondary halogenoalkanes undergo elimination by:

options.text: both E2 and E1, according to the choice of solvent

blocks.explanation: Secondary halogenoalkanes can show both E2 and E1 according to the choice of the solvent (21.3.2).

book_ref.quote: secondary halogenoalkanes can show both E2 and E1 reactions according to the choice of the solvent

blocks.prompt: 81 When the hydroxide ion acts as a base on bromoethane, the organic product is:
blocks.explanation: As a base OH⁻ removes the β-hydrogen and the halogen to give an alkene; bromoethane gives ethene (21.4).

book_ref.quote: As a base, it removes both the β-hydrogen atom and the halogen atom to give an elimination product

blocks.prompt: 82 Bromoethane reacts with aqueous NaOH by substitution to give:
blocks.explanation: CH₃CH₂Br + NaOH (aqueous) → CH₃CH₂OH + NaBr (21.4).

book_ref.quote: Substitution reaction: bromoethane and aqueous sodium hydroxide

blocks.prompt: 83 Bromoethane heated with NaOH in alcohol gives mainly:
blocks.explanation: With NaOH in alcohol, elimination occurs: CH₃CH₂Br + NaOH → CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O + NaBr (21.4).

book_ref.quote: Elimination reaction: bromoethane and sodium hydroxide in alcohol

blocks.prompt: 84 The reaction of a halogenoalkane with sodium hydroxide is carried out under reflux in order to:

options.text: convert the alkene into an alcohol
avoid the loss of volatile products at the higher temperature

blocks.explanation: The reaction takes place at higher temperature under reflux conditions to avoid the loss of volatile products (21.4).

book_ref.quote: The reaction takes place at higher temperature under reflux conditions to avoid the loss of volatile products

blocks.prompt: 85 Cyanide ion, CN⁻, gives mainly a substitution product with halogenoalkanes because it is:

options.text: a strong nucleophile but a weak base
a strong base but a weak nucleophile

blocks.explanation: CN⁻ is a strong nucleophile but a weak base, so it gives a substitution product, a nitrile (21.4 ii).

book_ref.quote: is a strong nucleophile but a weak base

blocks.prompt: 86 Bromoethane reacts with ethanolic potassium cyanide to give:
blocks.explanation: CH₃CH₂Br + KCN → CH₃CH₂C≡N + KBr; bromoethane gives propane nitrile (21.4 ii).

book_ref.quote: Bromoethane reacts with potassium cyanide to give propane nitrile

blocks.prompt: 87 The reaction of a halogenoalkane with KCN is typically carried out by:

options.text: passing KCN vapour over the halide in light
heating with ethanolic KCN under reflux
adding anhydrous FeCl₃ at room temperature

blocks.explanation: The halogenoalkane is heated with an ethanolic solution of potassium cyanide under reflux (21.4 ii).

book_ref.quote: heating the halogenoalkane with an ethanolic solution of potassium cyanide under reflux

blocks.prompt: 88 Bromoethane has two carbon atoms. The number of carbon atoms in the nitrile it forms with KCN is:
blocks.explanation: The CN group adds one carbon: CH₃CH₂Br → CH₃CH₂C≡N (propanenitrile, 3 C) (21.4 ii).

book_ref.quote: so it reacts with halogenoalkanes to give substitution product, a nitrile

blocks.prompt: 89 Ammonia, acting as a nucleophile, reacts with bromoethane to give first:
blocks.explanation: The lone pair on N of ammonia attacks the carbon of C₂H₅–Br; the product is ethylamine (ethanamine) H₂N–C₂H₅ + HBr (21.4 iii).

book_ref.quote: Ammonia and bromoethane (original drawing

blocks.prompt: 90 Different types of amines can be produced from a halogenoalkane and ammonia by:

options.text: carefully controlling the amounts of halogenoalkane and ammonia

blocks.explanation: Different types of amines can be produced if the amounts of halogenoalkane and ammonia are carefully controlled (21.4 iii).

book_ref.quote: Different types of amines can be produced if the amounts of halogenoalkane and ammonia are carefully controlled

blocks.prompt: 91 Ethanamine formed from ammonia and bromoethane can react further with bromoethane because:
blocks.explanation: Ethanamine is also a nucleophile and competes with ammonia, giving diethyl amine (N-ethylethanamine) (21.4 iii).

book_ref.quote: Since ethanamine is also a nucleophile, it can compete with ammonia

blocks.prompt: 92 N-Ethylethanamine, (C₂H₅)₂NH, reacts with bromoethane to give HBr and:
blocks.explanation: N-ethylethanamine attacks another bromoethane to give N,N-diethylethanamine + HBr (21.4 iii).

book_ref.quote: N-ethylethanamine and bromoethane (original drawing

blocks.prompt: 93 When a large excess of bromoethane reacts with ammonia, the final product may be:
blocks.explanation: With a large excess of bromoethane the reaction may proceed to the quaternary ammonium salt (21.4 iii).

book_ref.quote: If a large excess of bromoethane is used, the reaction may proceed to give quaternary ammonium salt

blocks.prompt: 94 With a large excess of bromoethane, N,N-diethylethanamine gives a quaternary ammonium salt. Its nitrogen carries:

options.text: four ethyl groups and a positive charge
three ethyl groups and a lone pair
two ethyl groups and one H
one ethyl group and two H

blocks.explanation: (C₂H₅)₃N + C₂H₅Br → quaternary ammonium salt: N is bonded to four C₂H₅ groups and carries the positive charge; bromide is the counter-ion (21.4 iii).

book_ref.quote: If a large excess of bromoethane is used, the reaction may proceed to give quaternary ammonium salt as the final product

blocks.prompt: 95 In the silver nitrate test, the halogenoalkane is treated in a water–ethanol mixture. The ethanol is added to:
blocks.explanation: The alcohol in the water–ethanol mixture helps to dissolve the halogenoalkane; water is the nucleophile (21.4 iv).

book_ref.quote: the alcohol in this mixture helps to dissolve the halogenoalkane

blocks.prompt: 96 In the silver nitrate test, the halide ion is released from the halogenoalkane by:

options.text: silver ion acting as a nucleophile
nitrate ion acting as a base
ethanol acting as an oxidizing agent

blocks.explanation: CH₃CH₂X + H–OH → CH₃CH₂OH + H⁺ + X⁻; water replaces the halide ion as a nucleophile (21.4 iv).

book_ref.quote: Water reacts with halogenoalkane as a nucleophile replacing the halide ion

blocks.prompt: 97 A bromoalkane warmed with aqueous ethanolic silver nitrate gives a precipitate of:
blocks.explanation: Ag⁺ + Br⁻ → AgBr (cream yellow ppt) (21.4 iv).

book_ref.quote: a precipitate with a characteristic colour corresponding to the halide ion present

blocks.prompt: 98 In the silver nitrate test, a white precipitate shows that the halogenoalkane contains:
blocks.explanation: Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl (white ppt); the colour detects the halide ion present (21.4 iv).

book_ref.quote: Thus, the reaction helps to detect the halide ion present in halogenoalkanes

blocks.prompt: 99 The colour of the silver iodide precipitate formed in this test is:
blocks.explanation: Ag⁺ + I⁻ → AgI (bright yellow ppt) (21.4 iv).

book_ref.quote: The released halide ion then reacts with silver nitrate

blocks.prompt: 100 In the silver nitrate test, the speed of appearance of the precipitate indicates:

options.text: the reactivity of the halogenoalkane: quicker means more reactive
the boiling point of the halogenoalkane
the strength of the silver nitrate only

blocks.explanation: Comparing rates of formation of silver halides gives the reactivities; the quicker the precipitate, the more reactive the halogenoalkane (21.4 iv).

book_ref.quote: The quicker the precipitate appears, the more reactive is the halogenoalkane

blocks.prompt: 101 With aqueous ethanolic silver nitrate, which of these gives its precipitate most slowly?
blocks.explanation: An iodoalkane gives a precipitate much quicker than a bromoalkane; a chloroalkane reacts very slowly (21.4 iv).

book_ref.quote: A chloroalkane, however, reacts very slowly

blocks.prompt: 102 Bromobenzene is prepared from benzene and bromine in the presence of the catalyst:
blocks.explanation: Benzene reacts with chlorine or bromine in the presence of anhydrous FeCl₃ or FeBr₃ (21.5).

book_ref.quote: in the presence a of catalyst, anhydrous FeCl₃ or FeBr₃

blocks.prompt: 103 The preparation of chlorobenzene from benzene and chlorine is an example of:
blocks.explanation: The halogenation of benzene with a FeX₃ catalyst is called electrophilic aromatic substitution (21.5).

book_ref.quote: The reaction is called electrophilic aromatic substitution reaction

blocks.prompt: 104 The halogenation of benzene to give halogenoarenes is typically carried out:

options.text: at room temperature with anhydrous FeX₃

blocks.explanation: The reaction is typically carried out at room temperature with anhydrous FeCl₃ or FeBr₃ (21.5).

book_ref.quote: is typically carried out at room temperature

blocks.prompt: 105 Besides the halobenzene, the other product of C₆H₆ + X₂ (with FeX₃) is:
blocks.explanation: C₆H₆ + X₂ → C₆H₅X + HX; an H of benzene is replaced by X (21.5).

blocks.prompt: 106 Halogenoalkanes are:

options.text: aliphatic compounds with the halogen attached to an alkyl group
aromatic compounds with halogen on a benzene ring
alkenes with a halogen on the double bond

blocks.explanation: Halogenoalkanes are aliphatic organic compounds in which the halogen atom is attached to an alkyl group (21.5.1).

book_ref.quote: Halogenoalkanes are aliphatic organic compounds in which halogen atom is attached with an alkyl group

blocks.prompt: 107 In chlorobenzene, a lone pair of electrons on chlorine is:
blocks.explanation: The electron pair on chlorine is delocalised due to the involvement of the chlorine lone pair with the aromatic ring (21.5.1).

book_ref.quote: the electron pair on the chlorine atom is delocalised due to the involvement of the chlorine lone pair with the aromatic ring

blocks.prompt: 108 The C—Cl bond in chlorobenzene is stronger than in chloroethane because it has:
blocks.explanation: Delocalisation of the chlorine lone pair gives the C—Cl bond partial double-bond character, so it is stronger and harder to break (21.5.1).

book_ref.quote: The carbon-halogen bond is stronger due to the partial double-bond character

blocks.prompt: 109 Because of the stronger carbon–halogen bond, halogenoarenes are:

options.text: less reactive and synthetically less useful

blocks.explanation: The C—Cl bond becomes difficult to break; consequently halogenoarenes are less reactive and synthetically less useful (21.5.1).

book_ref.quote: the halogenoarenes, are less reactive and synthetically less useful

blocks.prompt: 110 In halogenoalkanes, the attack of a base on a hydrogen of the carbon adjacent to the C–X carbon gives:
blocks.explanation: The attack by bases on the hydrogen of the adjacent carbon gives another important class of reactions, elimination reactions (21.5.1).

book_ref.quote: The attack by bases on the hydrogen atom attached with the carbon atom adjacent to it

blocks.prompt: 111 The use of DDT as a pesticide has been restricted or banned in developed countries because of:
blocks.explanation: Halogen compounds like DDT have been used as pesticides, but their persistence in the environment led to restrictions or bans (21.5.1 box).

book_ref.quote: their persistence in the environment has led to restrictions or banning of their use

blocks.prompt: 112 Some developing countries saw a sharp increase in malaria deaths after DDT was removed because DDT is:

options.text: a cheap and effective mosquito control agent

blocks.explanation: DDT is a cheap and effective mosquito control agent, so its removal raised malaria deaths in some developing countries (21.5.1 box).

book_ref.quote: Because DDT is a cheap and effective mosquito control agent
